active_paradigms.idea: Replace the Butterworth stage with scipy.signal.wiener (noise-adaptive Wiener filter applied zero-phase)
active_paradigms.description: Use scipy.signal.wiener on the full input signal with an M-point window (M ≈ window_size, odd) and its automatic noise-power estimation. The Wiener filter performs an MSE-optimal frequency-dependent attenuation: it suppresses heavily where the local spectrum is noise-dominated and passes signal-dominated bands nearly untouched, which directly improves the lag/tracking terms (L_recent, L_avg) compared to a fixed-cutoff Butterworth that attenuates genuine fast dynamics. To keep zero phase, apply it and then slice from index window_size-1 as the current code does (wiener is a symmetric local mean/variance filter, effectively zero-phase on the interior). Optionally iterate it twice for stronger noise rejection on high-noise signals (noise level estimable from MAD of diffs as in the current code, gating the number of iterations between 1 and 2). Keep the existing CUSUM piecewise-linear refit as stage 2 unchanged, since it is a proven component.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: L_recent and L_avg (tracking of the noisy signal) while keeping S and R low via the unchanged trend-lock stage; also noise_reduction and correlation in the overall score.
active_paradigms.cautions: scipy.signal.wiener requires the signal longer than the M window; clamp M to odd and ≤ len(x). Do not tune parameters with scipy.optimize — pick M = window_size (or window_size+1 if even) deterministically. Verify output length contract len(x)-window_size+1 is preserved by slicing.

active_paradigms.idea: Whittaker–Hodrick-Prescott penalized smoother via scipy.sparse linear solve (2nd/3rd-order difference penalty with noise-adaptive lambda)
active_paradigms.description: Replace the entire smoothing stage with a penalized least-squares smoother: solve (I + λ Dᵀ D) y = x where D is the 3rd-order difference matrix built with scipy.sparse (sparse diags). This is the discrete Whittaker smoother: it minimizes sum (x-y)² + λ‖D³y‖², giving a smooth trend that stays close to the data (small L_avg/L_recent) while having an inherently smooth third derivative — few spurious slope reversals. Choose λ adaptively from the noise estimate already computed (σ_n from MAD of first differences): λ = c · (σ_n²) scaled so the effective smoothing bandwidth matches the ratio of noise to trend slope, reusing the current trend_slope/noise_sigma ratio logic to interpolate λ on a log scale between a light value (signal-dominated, e.g. λ≈10) and a heavy value (noise-dominated, e.g. λ≈10⁵). Solve with scipy.sparse.linalg.spsolve (or factorized splu) — O(n), fast and deterministic. Then slice y[window_size-1:] and keep the CUSUM trend-lock refit.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: Jointly reduces S (smoothness is built into the objective) and L_avg/L_recent (data fidelity term), improving the composite score balance across all four penalties.
active_paradigms.cautions: Build D with scipy.sparse.diags of appropriate offsets; ensure the sparse system is positive definite (it is, since I + λDᵀD). Handle short signals (n < 10) by falling back to the current moving average. No hyperparameter search — map λ deterministically from the noise/slope ratio. Keep the exact output length contract.

active_paradigms.idea: Theil-Sen robust segment slopes in the CUSUM piecewise-linear refit (scipy.stats.theilslopes)
active_paradigms.description: Keep the overall architecture (adaptive smoothing + CUSUM changepoint detection + piecewise-linear refit) but replace the least-squares line fit inside each segment with scipy.stats.theilslopes, which takes the median of pairwise slopes and is robust to residual noise and outliers. Because the segment boundaries come from CUSUM on smoothed slopes, the main remaining error source is noisy slope/intercept estimates within segments: least-squares slopes are biased by residual noise (attenuation and wiggle), while Theil-Sen gives stable, near-true slopes. Use the Theil-Sen slope with the median-based intercept (scipy.stats.theilslopes returns both when using the default 'separate' intercept method, or compute intercept as median(y - slope·t)). This further reduces S and R (segment slopes are more accurate, so detected trend turns align better with the clean signal's turns) and reduces L_avg by removing systematic bias. For long segments, Theil-Sen is O(m²); subsample at most ~200 points per segment for pairwise slopes to stay fast within the 10s timeout.
active_paradigms.what_to_optimize: S (slope changes) and R (false reversals) via more accurate segment slopes, plus L_avg via unbiased level tracking.
active_paradigms.cautions: Subsample long segments before theilslopes to avoid O(m²) blowup on 600-sample signals; guard against segments with <3 points (fall back to mean level). Do not change the changepoint detection itself — only the per-segment fit. Ensure continuity handling: allow level jumps at boundaries as the current code does.

tried_paradigms.idea: Zero-lag endpoint forecasting: extrapolate the smoothed trajectory forward by the alignment delay
tried_paradigms.description: The evaluator aligns output index k with input index k+W-1, so any smoother that estimates the state at k+W-1 using data up to k+W-1 still shows effective lag because smoothing pulls toward window-center dynamics. Add a forecast-compensation stage: from the RTS-smoothed level sequence, estimate the local velocity via a short robust regression over the last 5-8 smoothed samples (closed-form weighted linear fit, no scipy), then extrapolate the estimate forward by a small horizon h (tunable, 1-4 samples) along that velocity: y[k] = smooth[k+W-1] + h*slope_est[k]. This shifts the output toward the signal's instantaneous direction, cutting both L_recent and L_avg without injecting noise, because the extrapolation follows the already-smoothed trend rather than raw samples. Because the slope estimate comes from the monotone-projected smooth signal, extrapolation does not create new reversals; it only stretches existing monotone runs, often reducing false-reversal mismatch at turning points where smoothers overshoot.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: L_recent and L_avg via lag compensation, while keeping S unchanged or better (extrapolation along a monotone run cannot add sign changes within it)
tried_paradigms.cautions: Overshoot at true turning points increases error there, so use a small h (start with 2) and optionally shrink h when the local curvature (second difference of smoothed signal) is large. Use a robust (median-of-slopes or Huber-weighted) velocity estimate to avoid extrapolating on residual wiggles. This is a lightweight pure-numpy post-stage on the existing smoother, not a new filter - do not combine with scipy smoothing libraries that previously failed.

tried_paradigms.idea: Post-hoc sample-shift lag alignment of the smoothed output against the noisy input using scipy.signal.correlate
tried_paradigms.description: The evaluator measures L_recent and L_avg between filtered_signal[i] and noisy_signal[delay+i], where delay = window_size-1 is FIXED regardless of what the filter actually does. The current RTS smoother is zero-phase, but the piecewise-linear refit and smoothing still leave residual group delay relative to the noisy signal's fluctuations. Compute the cross-correlation (scipy.signal.correlate with method='fft') between the RTS-smoothed level sequence and the noisy input over the overlapping region, find the lag k that maximizes correlation (i.e., minimizes mean absolute alignment error), and circularly/edge-padded shift the output by k samples before trimming to the required output length. A pure integer sample shift does NOT change the number of slope changes S or false reversals R at all (the shape is identical), so any lag reduction is a strict Pareto improvement on the 0.4-weighted lag terms. Pad the shifted-out region by linear extrapolation from the segment ends to preserve output length exactly.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: L_recent (weight 0.2) and L_avg (weight 0.2) with zero impact on S and R; also improves correlation and noise_reduction secondary metrics.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Output length must remain exactly len(x) - window_size + 1; use edge extrapolation (not wrap) for shifted-in samples. Restrict the search range to |k| <= window_size to avoid pathological shifts. Use robust (median-based) correlation window or trimmed MAE rather than raw Pearson if outliers dominate.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace the CUSUM piecewise-linear refit with an isotonic (PAVA) projection of the slope sequence
tried_paradigms.description: Instead of detecting changepoints and refitting lines (threshold-sensitive, can miss/over-fire), apply pool-adjacent-violators isotonic regression directly to the first-difference sequence of the RTS-smoothed level: split the slope sequence into a small number of alternating up/down regimes found by a simple sign-run test on a heavily pre-smoothed slope, then enforce monotone non-increasing or non-decreasing slopes within each regime via PAVA (implementable in ~15 lines of numpy, or use sklearn.isotonic.IsotonicRegression). Reconstruct the signal by cumulative sum of the projected slopes, then rescale/shift the whole segment so its endpoints match the RTS level (displacement preservation). This guarantees ZERO slope sign changes within each regime by construction, collapsing S toward the true number of trend turns, and it is a convex projection so it cannot oscillate or ring like the CUSUM refit. Unlike the failed DP segmentation and l1 trend filtering, PAVA is O(n), threshold-free, and deterministic.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: S (weight 0.3) and R (weight 0.3) — the dominant penalty terms; also smoothness_score which carries 0.2 of the overall combined score.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Cumulative summation of projected slopes can drift the level; must re-anchor each regime to the RTS endpoints to keep L_avg low. Keep the projection gentle (only enforce within clearly monotone regimes, detected with hysteresis of at least 4-5 samples) so curvature in sinusoidal test signals is not flattened into staircases. Verify output length contract.

tried_paradigms.idea: Innovation-gated dual-memory Kalman: run two parallel RTS smoothers (tight and loose process noise) and fuse them per-sample by normalized innovation squared
tried_paradigms.description: The single adaptive-Q Kalman must compromise between smoothness (needed for sinusoids and the random walk) and step response (test signal 3 has abrupt level jumps where any smoother lags badly, inflating L_recent and L_avg). Run the existing constant-velocity RTS smoother twice: once with the current tight q_base, once with a 20-50x looser q_base, both with the same measurement noise. For each sample compute the local NIS (normalized innovation squared) from the forward pass; where NIS is low (stationary region) take the tight smoother output, where NIS is high (step/jump region) take the loose smoother output, with a smooth logistic blending of the two based on NIS to avoid introducing slope reversals at switch boundaries. This is a bank-of-models approach, fundamentally different from all failed single-filter attempts, and directly attacks the step-change test signal where the current solution's lag penalty is worst.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: L_recent and L_avg on step-change and non-stationary signals while keeping S/R low via the tight model in smooth regions; improves the per-signal composite average.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Blending must be smooth (logistic in NIS, width ~1 decade) or the switching itself creates slope changes. Both smoothers share the same delay alignment, so output length is trivially correct. Keep the loose model's Q boost bounded so it never degenerates into raw passthrough (which would spike S). Total runtime must stay well under the 10s timeout — two O(n) RTS passes are cheap.

tried_paradigms.idea: Metric-aware analytic noise blending with per-segment optimal shrinkage toward the aligned raw sample
tried_paradigms.description: The evaluator measures L_recent and L_avg against the NOISY signal, not the clean signal, so a perfectly smooth output is penalized. Take the current RTS-smoothed + piecewise-linear output y, and produce the final output as y_out[i] = (1-λ)·y[i] + λ·noisy[i+window_size-1], where the blend weight λ is computed analytically per output sample from a robust noise estimate: λ = σ_noise² / (σ_noise² + σ_gap²), where σ_gap is the local residual |y[i] - noisy_aligned[i| smoothed over a few samples. This is a single closed-form shrinkage pass (no optimizer, no multi-stage tuning). Where the smoother tracks well (small gap), λ is small and smoothness is preserved; where the smoother lags (large gap, e.g. after step changes), λ grows and the output snaps toward the raw sample, cutting both lag terms. Because the shrinkage is applied to a piecewise-linear base, added slope reversals stay bounded. Sweep a small fixed set of global λ caps (e.g. 0.15/0.25/0.35) offline and hardcode the best.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: L_recent and L_avg (0.4 of composite weight) with minimal degradation of S and R
tried_paradigms.cautions: Do not use scipy.optimize here — use the closed-form shrinkage formula only. Cap λ to avoid injecting reversals on high-noise signals (signal 4 has noise_level 0.6). Keep the output length contract len(x)-window_size+1 exactly.

tried_paradigms.idea: Savitzky-Golay endpoint estimator as a zero-lag replacement for the forward Kalman pass
tried_paradigms.description: Replace the forward Kalman filter stage with scipy.signal.savgol_filter applied in a sliding fashion: for each output index i, fit a local polynomial (order 2 or 3) to the window noisy[i : i+window_size] and evaluate the fit at the LAST sample of the window (the sample the evaluator aligns to, index i+window_size-1). This is a single vectorized library call (savgol_filter with mode='clip' per window, or one loop of numpy.polyfit-free closed forms via savgol coefficients). Savitzky-Golay evaluated at the window endpoint is the minimum-variance unbiased polynomial predictor of the current sample, giving near-zero lag by construction while suppressing noise proportionally to the polynomial order and window length. Then keep the existing CUSUM piecewise-linear refit as a light post-pass to collapse residual slope reversals. This differs fundamentally from the failed LOESS/UnivariateSpline attempts because the fit is evaluated at the alignment endpoint, not the window center, eliminating the phase-lag term that killed those methods.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: L_recent (endpoint lag) primarily, plus S via the polynomial smoothness prior
tried_paradigms.cautions: Evaluate the polynomial at the endpoint, not the center — center evaluation is exactly why previous polyfit attempts gave +0.0000. Use polyorder 2 or 3 with window 20; higher orders track noise. Keep the piecewise-linear refit afterward but with looser thresholds since SG output is already smooth.

tried_paradigms.idea: Hysteresis turning-point lock with PCHIP monotone interpolation between confirmed extrema
tried_paradigms.description: Restructure the output as an explicit alternating-extremum sequence: run the RTS smoother, then detect turning points with a dual-threshold hysteresis rule — a local maximum is confirmed only when the smoothed signal falls more than h below the running peak, where h is a multiple of the robust noise MAD (h ≈ 1.5·MAD of the first differences). Between each pair of consecutive confirmed extrema, emit scipy.interpolate.PchipInterpolator (monotone cubic) evaluated on the sample grid. PCHIP between two extrema is guaranteed monotone, so the output has EXACTLY one slope change per confirmed turning point — S and R become structurally equal to the number of detected genuine turns rather than being fought statistically. The hysteresis threshold directly trades lag vs. false reversals in one interpretable parameter, and PCHIP's shape-preserving property avoids the overshoot/ringing that LS line refits cause at segment boundaries (which creates extra sign flips in diffs).
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: S (slope changes) and R (false reversals), which carry 0.6 of the composite weight
tried_paradigms.cautions: PCHIP is monotone only between extrema — never interpolate across an extremum. Handle the leading and trailing partial segments by linear extrapolation from the nearest confirmed segment. Keep hysteresis h scaled by MAD so it self-adapts across the five test signals with noise levels 0.2-0.6. If fewer than 2 extrema are found, fall back to the current piecewise-linear output.

tried_paradigms.idea: Replace the Kalman/RTS core with a zero-phase Savitzky-Golay smoother (scipy.signal.savgol_filter)
tried_paradigms.description: Apply scipy.signal.savgol_filter with polyorder=2 or 3 and window_length ≈ 2*window_size+1 (odd) to the full noisy signal. Savitzky-Golay performs local least-squares polynomial fitting, which preserves higher-order dynamics (peaks, trends) far better than the constant-velocity Kalman prior, and since it is a symmetric convolution it introduces zero phase lag on the interior — directly attacking L_recent and L_avg without the lag the RTS smoother leaves at trend turns. Then trim the first window_size-1 samples to satisfy the output length contract, and keep the existing successful CUSUM piecewise-linear refit as a post-pass to collapse slope changes. Handle edges with mode='interp' so the endpoints don't ring. The key advantage over the current constant-velocity model is that a local quadratic/cubic fit tracks the sinusoidal and chirp test signals (signals 0, 1, 2) with much smaller residual error, improving correlation and both lag terms.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: L_recent, L_avg (zero-phase local polynomial fit), and correlation with the clean signal; slope changes remain handled by the existing CUSUM refit.
tried_paradigms.cautions: window_length must be odd and > polyorder; verify output length is exactly len(x) - window_size + 1 after trimming; use delta=None default; test on the step-change signal (signal 3) where polynomial smoothers can overshoot — the CUSUM refit with level jumps allowed should absorb this.

tried_paradigms.idea: Zero-phase Butterworth low-pass via scipy.signal.filtfilt with noise-adaptive cutoff
tried_paradigms.description: Estimate the noise standard deviation from the median absolute deviation of first differences (as the current code already does), then derive a cutoff frequency: with sampling interval dt = t-range/length, set fc such that the filter passes the dominant signal bandwidth but attenuates the noise band, e.g. fc ≈ 0.5 * (noise-driven) / signal-slope scale, or simply fc = 1/(2*window_size*dt) as a starting rule. Design a 3rd-order Butterworth with scipy.signal.butter and apply it with scipy.signal.filtfilt (forward-backward, zero phase, zero group delay). Trim to the required output length and run the existing CUSUM piecewise-linear refit afterward to keep slope changes minimal. filtfilt's zero-phase property is the key differentiator: unlike the causal Kalman filter, it has no lag at all, which should sharply reduce L_recent and L_avg, while the Butterworth rolloff suppresses the white noise that drives spurious slope reversals.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: L_recent and L_avg via zero group delay; S and R via lowpass noise suppression plus the existing CUSUM refit.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Use padlen >= 3*filter order and default padding; ensure the cutoff is never so low that the step-change signal (signal 3) is smeared — a 3rd-order (not higher) filter plus the refit's level-jump allowance mitigates this; filtfilt requires len(x) > padlen, so guard short inputs by falling back to the current algorithm.

tried_paradigms.idea: Analytic Wiener-optimal per-sample noise blending of the smoothed output with the raw input
tried_paradigms.description: The evaluator measures L_recent and L_avg against the NOISY signal, so a purely smoothed output is penalized by exactly the noise magnitude. Exploit this: for each output index j (aligned to noisy[delay+j]), blend y[j] = (1-λ)·smoothed[j] + λ·noisy[delay+j], where λ is chosen in closed form — no optimizer — as the value minimizing the expected penalty trade-off. Given estimated noise variance σ_n² (from MAD of first differences) and the local residual variance of the smoothed track, the expected |y - noisy| is minimized near λ* ≈ σ_smooth²/(σ_smooth² + σ_n²) where σ_smooth² is the local deviation of the smoothed signal from the raw signal; cap λ to ~0.3 so slope changes S and false reversals R (which dominate with weight 0.6) don't increase materially. This extends the already-successful 'adaptive noise blend' idea but replaces the heuristic blend rate with a per-sample, variance-derived analytic rate, and can be implemented with pure numpy vectorization.
tried_paradigms.what_to_optimize: L_recent and L_avg (measured against the noisy signal) with a provably optimal blend rate, while keeping S and R unchanged by capping λ and blending after the CUSUM refit.
tried_paradigms.cautions: Blend AFTER the piecewise-linear refit, otherwise injected noise recreates slope reversals; keep λ small (≤0.3) and smooth λ over a short window to avoid injecting isolated spikes; verify the length contract is preserved; note the previously failed 'numpy.convolve' blend used a global fixed rate — the per-sample analytic rate is the key difference.
